### Software stocks spared in tech rout as AI narrative shifts
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/74b9654424d4921d
- Primary Source: Financial Times (https://www.ft.com/content/90b82a64-4f58-45d7-8a6a-4c2730545b65)
- Executive Summary: Investors are rotating away from semiconductor dominance toward software firms possessing proprietary datasets and entrenched customer bases. Despite early 2026 sell-offs driven by fears of AI-driven obsolescence, the software sector now exhibits greater defensive value amidst broader tech market volatility.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Institutional investors including Deutsche Bank, Barclays, and Man Group (Global technology equity markets): Capital rotation from semiconductor hardware into defensive, data-moat-heavy software firms
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Shift in AI investment thesis from infrastructure-first to sustainable software application value
* [Market & Financial Detail] Market sentiment shifting from AI hardware infrastructure to software application utility.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Software firms with data moats and high retention re-emerging as structural winners.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Semiconductor and software stocks are neck-and-neck in market performance so far this year following a sharp turnaround in sentiment about the winners and losers of the AI boom, as a bruising tech sell-off upends this year’s popular trades.
> Software shares have been relatively unscathed by this month’s brutal rout in the tech sector, which has been concentrated in the semiconductor stocks that until recently were investor darlings.
> “The sentiment on semis is now exactly the sentiment we had on software six to nine months ago,” said Max Uleer, head of cross-asset strategy at Deutsche Bank.
> Investors dumped the stocks of software companies earlier this year on fears that advances in AI technology would undermine their business models. But the sector reversed those losses in the second half of the year and has held on to its gains in the recent volatility, highlighting a shift in how investors are thinking about the market impact of the AI revolution.
> “Undeniably, the narrative has moved for software as a sector, which was perceived as universally challenging, into a defined group of those who will be the structural winners and those who will not,” said Lawrence Jamieson, co-head of Emea equity capital markets at Barclays.
> Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group, said: “The view from 40,000 feet is that markets don’t know who the winners and losers [from AI] will ultimately be.”
> She said 2026 had been “a guessing game, where investors have made somewhat snap judgments, like the assumption that software firms and their products would become obsolete”.
> “The thinking has evolved over time to questioning that thesis and ultimately worrying about semiconductors,” she added.
> The software and semiconductor sub-indices of the S&P 500 are now both marginally negative year-to-date, with software stocks outperforming semiconductors.
> The software sell-off at the start of 2026 gathered speed after the release of new tools by AI lab Anthropic, which gave users the ability to more easily perform complex legal, sales and marketing functions.
> As the sell-off deepened, being overweight semiconductor stocks compared to benchmarks while being underweight software stocks became a hedge fund favourite trade earlier this year.
> But the worst of the fears for the software sector have since faded, with investors reassured by the defensive value of companies’ large customer bases and their perceived “moats” of proprietary data sets.
> “Not all software businesses are created equal,” said Ben Preston, global equity strategist at Orbis Investments. “While some face genuine disruption, others possess proprietary data, embedded customer relationships and specialist expertise that AI cannot easily replicate.”

### Microsoft says state-backed hacking groups in China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added AI penetration testing tool ARTEX to their arsenals (Jonathan Greig/The Record)
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/e7f2fb770e8efb3e
- Primary Source: The Record (https://therecord.media/microsoft-china-salt-typhoon-using-artex-ai-tool)
- Executive Summary: Microsoft reports that state-sponsored hacking groups, including Salt Typhoon, have integrated the AI-powered penetration testing tool ARTEX into their offensive arsenals. By automating reconnaissance, credential theft, and vulnerability scanning, the tool compresses intrusion cycles to minutes while bypassing static signature detection via behavioral obfuscation.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Microsoft Security Intelligence, Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon: Utilization of the AI platform ARTEX for automated network reconnaissance and privileged access
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] AI-enabled automation significantly accelerates intrusion timelines and evades traditional signature-based detection
* [Key Fact Detail] ARTEX enables multi-stage automated attacks, significantly compressing intrusion cycles.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Behavioral analysis emerges as the only viable defense against AI-driven intrusion.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> State-backed hacking groups in China and North Korea are using a powerful AI hacking tool in attacks, according to a new report from Microsoft.
> Microsoft explained that state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers are using Artex, an AI-powered platform that can automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed.
> The study emerged hours after The New York Times and NextGov reported that Artex was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
> Microsoft said on Wednesday that Chinese state-backed groups Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon have integrated Artex into their suite of tools, using it for “network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation.”
> “In the past few weeks, we’ve reported several distinct campaigns that abused Artex to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation,” Microsoft explained.
> Salt Typhoon is a prolific Chinese hacking group that U.S. agencies believe was behind the breach of at least nine telecommunications giants in 2024. The hack alarmed White House officials in 2024 because it allegedly gave China’s hackers access to communications from the phones of President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as well as several Democratic leaders.
> Salt Typhoon was also accused of attacking several European governments and critical infrastructure organizations globally.
> Artex was released in July, and according to Microsoft, it has been steadily added to the arsenal of multiple North Korean and Chinese groups.
> Artex allows threat actors to define specific goals and use AI agents to attack targets. Microsoft said Artex “can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes.”
> “ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques. ARTEX does sometimes transmit distinctive characteristics associated with its integrated penetration testing tools,” Microsoft explained.
> “However, threat actors using ARTEX can and do vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking. The most reliable and durable signal of ARTEX activity is behavioral: ARTEX sends a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retries variations on the same technique or moves on to next-stage actions at machine speed.”
> By default, Artex does not take measures to hide its activity, the researchers added.

### Nvidia halts chip shipments to south-east Asia
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/72121f63fa770ad5
- Primary Source: Financial Times (https://www.ft.com/content/7838a715-07d4-4605-aa60-21f5af2b2370)
- Executive Summary: Nvidia has instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia to comply with new US export control regulations. This measure targets the loophole allowing Chinese AI developers to access restricted high-end GPU compute via local cloud providers, as firms struggle with the lack of specific compliance guidelines.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Nvidia, Dell, Supermicro, US Department of Commerce: Halting server shipments and conducting compliance audits to adhere to new US compute export restrictions
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To prevent Chinese entities from bypassing sanctions via third-party cloud rental services
* [Key Metrics] The chipmaker booked $104bn of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent increase in 12 months, according to company accounts.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Industry impact: SE Asian compute hubs face immediate supply chain disruption and high compliance verification costs.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to four south-east Asian countries, as the US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.
> Manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia’s chips into servers, have told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not allow their orders to be shipped, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.
> It is unclear whether the halt is temporary, as Nvidia and its partners try to work out how to comply with Washington’s new export controls, the people said.
> The four south-east Asian countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips, whose exports are restricted by Washington.
> The region is lucrative for Nvidia. The chipmaker booked $104bn of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent increase in 12 months, according to company accounts. Nvidia also records some of its Taiwan and China revenue via its Singapore unit.
> Many Chinese groups get around US export controls by renting access through cloud computing providers that buy servers containing Nvidia chips.
> The US commerce department introduced new rules last week aimed at stopping the practice. The measures came after Jensen Huang was briefly ousted as chief executive of Nvidia following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman tied to a cloud provider that leased access to Chinese companies and is being investigated for alleged involvement in smuggling.
> The revelations complicated Huang’s stance that the US should continue selling Nvidia chips to Chinese companies to increase their dependence on American technology.
> Despite Beijing’s push to develop domestic alternatives, China’s leading AI labs remain heavily reliant on Nvidia’s processors to develop their flagship models, particularly during compute-intensive early-stage training.
> While many were hoping Huang’s return to the helm of Nvidia this week would open a path to less strict enforcement of the new rules, there is little indication that the company will hold back from executing them, said the people.
> The commerce department has set a 90-day deadline for cloud providers to obtain a licence by proving that their end users do not include restricted entities.
> “There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” said an executive at a cloud provider. “No one knows how to apply for this licence while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”
> Demand from Chinese tech companies has fuelled south-east Asia’s data centre boom, particularly in Malaysia and Indonesia, where billions of dollars have poured into the construction of AI infrastructure. The new US ...

### Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness Tells Investors It Lost 65% in Third Quarter
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/04b302a8f502f92c
- Primary Source: Wall Street Journal (https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/aschenbrenners-situational-awareness-tells-investors-it-lost-65-in-third-quarter-de8e9797?st=AGLTi8&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink)
- Executive Summary: Situational Awareness, a hedge fund founded by Leopold Aschenbrenner, reported a 65% net loss for Q3 following a liquidity crisis triggered by aggressive leveraged bets on the AI sector in July. The fund, which was forced to sell a significant portion of its public equity portfolio to Citadel to stave off implosion, is now pivoting toward more conservative risk management.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Leopold Aschenbrenner, Founder of Situational Awareness: 65% Q3 loss, shifting to more measured risk management
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] High leverage in AI bets caused margin calls during July market volatility
* [Key Metrics] 65% Q3 loss; fund faced margin calls in July.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Founder pivoting to more conservative risk management strategy.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Leopold Aschenbrenner, whose Situational Awareness hedge fund nearly unraveled over the summer after its borrowing-fueled bets on artificial intelligence soured, told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter as it worked to learn from its mistakes.
> The fund is up 88.5% after fees for the year through September, Aschenbrenner said in an investor letter seen by The Wall Street Journal, telling clients that investing opportunities today “are the highest potential return we have seen in the lifetime of the fund.”
> (Bloomberg) -- Situational Awareness told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter, after highly levered bets on artificial intelligence firms nearly led to the hedge fund’s implosion in July, according to the Wall Street Journal.
> The hedge fund is still up 88.5% after fees for the year through the month of September, founder Leopold Aschenbrenner said in a letter viewed by the Wall Street Journal. Despite the tumult, the fund stills sees opportunities to invest with high potential for return, according to the report.
> Situational Awareness was pushed to the brink in July as a brief moment of panic about AI spread across global markets, sparking margin calls from banks and turning it into a symbol of the wild swings that have accompanied the AI trade. The firm ultimately sold a large chunk of its public equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel.
> Aschenbrenner, who named his firm after a viral essay he wrote in 2024, has focused on firms he thinks will benefit from the AI revolution. He quickly became known for using leverage to ramp up his returns and his risks.
> Aschenbrenner said in the letter that he was taking a more measured approach to risk management, having learned a lesson from the recent turmoil. “Volatility, yes; existential risk, even if we are totally wrong, never,” he reportedly told investors.
> The third quarter performance referenced in the letter does not capture the more recent selloff in the market during the month of October, when valuations of AI companies came under scrutiny and wild swings in stocks tied to the artificial intelligence buildout have made it an even more complicated market for investors to navigate.
> Aschenbrenner wrote in the letter that Situational Awareness’s portfolio was composed of about 70% publicly traded stocks and 30% positions in private companies following the IPO of Anthropic, its largest private position, according to the report. The firm may rebalance its portfolio away from Anthropic, though it’s “highly bullish” at the IPO price, the WSJ reported.
> More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com

- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/6296aa29fbdcec94
- Primary Source: CBS News (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-jensen-huang-nvidia-ceo-reinstated/)
- Executive Summary: President Trump and VP Vance engaged with Nvidia's board and counsel to confirm Jensen Huang is not a target of DOJ investigations and poses no national security risks, facilitating his reinstatement as CEO. This intervention aimed to stabilize Nvidia's share price and secure the strategic continuity of a cornerstone in the U.S. AI supply chain.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] President Donald Trump, VP JD Vance, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, Nvidia Board: Provided legal and regulatory assurances to the board to facilitate Huang's return
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To prevent a market crash of the critical AI infrastructure provider and ensure U.S. technological dominance
* [Market & Financial Detail] Nvidia's market volatility due to the CEO's resignation prompted direct White House intervention.
* [Official Stance & Demand] The incident highlights Nvidia's status as a critical strategic asset in the U.S. AI infrastructure.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> President Trump made it clear to advisers on Friday: He wanted Jensen Huang back at Nvidia.
> It had been less than two weeks since the computing giant's CEO and founder had resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose firm had allegedly funneled Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia's share price spiraled, imperiling a company whose semiconductors and financing deals have helped power the U.S. artificial intelligence boom.
> The president had been on the phone with various Wall Street and Silicon Valley titans. The main takeaway from those conversations: The U.S. needs a strong Nvidia.
> Mr. Trump was also privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.
> Nvidia's board chair told investors on Tuesday of last week that the company did not intend to reinstate Huang. But before the end of the week, the board was privately signaling to the White House that it was serious about bringing him back. Board members just wanted to examine it from all angles first.
> Huang's surprise comeback as CEO on Monday came after Trump and his team spent the weekend working on making it happen, in part by offering the Nvidia board a range of legal assurances about Huang. After the deal was done and the tech giant's shares surged, Mr. Trump publicly celebrated it, telling CNBC that he "convinced them" to rehire him.
> CBS News spoke with U.S. officials and others directly familiar with the negotiations about how the deal came together.
> ### Two days of assurances
> Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel. Huang privately shared with the White House that he felt the board wanted to bring him back, but would need to be assured that the U.S. government didn't think he was a national security risk.
> In phone calls, board members were told Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation, that the government had no legal issues with him, and that the administration wouldn't view his return to Nvidia's helm as a problem.
> But what about Alice Huang, they wanted to know. She's the woman with whom Huang had an affair, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed. The White House made it clear their assurances didn't extend to her.
> Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. The company was put on a U.S. trade blacklist this week, and it has been investigated by the Justice and Commerce departments.
> Trump, Vance and board members hashed over the next steps. The board wanted to know what Mr. Trump would say publicly. They wanted Attorney General Todd Blanche himself to confirm Huang wasn't under investigation...

The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Jagmeet Singh: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
* [Key Fact Detail] The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday.
* [Industry Analysis] An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
> The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
> That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.
> Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
> While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
> Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
> The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

### 2 California companies are buying Nvidia's most advanced chips. Those companies are actually Chinese-owned, a CBS News investigation reveals.
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/0906db57b6e47b6b
- Primary Source: CBS News (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/nvidia-china-ai-chips-computing-sales/)
- Executive Summary: Investigations reveal that several California-based NVIDIA partners are effectively controlled by Chinese firms, with executives linked to Chinese military institutions and blacklisted entities. These entities leverage their U.S. registration to procure high-end AI chips and circumvent export controls by rerouting hardware to China via third-party jurisdictions.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] China-controlled California-based tech firms, NVIDIA (U.S. export control environment): Circumventing export restrictions to acquire and resell high-end AI chips
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] High demand for computing power in China vs. U.S. technology blockade
* [Key Metrics] Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Significant gaps identified in current export control enforcement and supply chain traceability.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.
> One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
> Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.
> The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.
> "It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.
> C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.
> That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.
> But Megaspeed, national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?
> "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.

> Nuralink FDA approval: Elon Musk's Neuralink has won FDA clearance for LINK, a late-stage US trial of its N1 brain chip. Patients living with ALS could qualify to join the study.
> Elon Musk's Neuralink has secured clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to start LINK, a pivotal study of its brain chip. Sharing the update on X, the company said no other implanted brain-computer interface in the country has reached this stage of testing. The study follows Neuralink's work with over 30 people who already have the implant, and those diagnosed with ALS could be among the new candidates.
> The study page on Neuralink's website says the trial will measure two things: how safe the N1 Implant is, and how accurately users can operate digital devices with it. The chip powers Telepathy, an experimental product meant to give people with paralysis control of a computer using their thoughts. It picks up activity from the part of the brain that governs hand motion. When users picture moving their hand, the system converts those signals into pointer movement as well as left, right and middle clicks.
> Neuralink is accepting applications from people whose hand function has been affected by ALS, a spinal cord injury or a brain stem stroke. Applicants first speak with the study team over a 30-minute call. This is followed by two days of in-person health checks and brain scans, such as an MRI. Caregivers take part in discussions from the first meeting.
> A surgeon fits the N1 Implant while the patient is under general anaesthesia, while Neuralink's R1 Robot positions the ultra-thin threads. Patients are generally discharged within a day. Monitoring lasts two years, with reviews roughly 10 and 45 days after the procedure, followed by checks at three, six, 12 and 24 months. Neuralink covers travel and certain other expenses.

A coalition of 42 state attorneys general, led by California AG Rob Bonta and Connecticut AG William Tong, is challenging this move, citing breaches of privacy commitments and potential violations of state chatbot safety laws effective January 2027.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Character.ai (Bankrupt entity), Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Bidder), Rob Bonta (CA AG) (U.S. Bankruptcy Court proceedings): Auction of 21 million user chat logs and personal data; AGs seeking injunction

> What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.
> Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
> The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.
> Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)
> Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.
> The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.
> In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.
> “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
> Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.
> “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer...

### Hands-on with the "Install as app" feature for Claude artifacts: they are HTML apps wrapped inside an Electron shim, which is managed via the main Claude app (Federico Viticci/MacStories)
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/4b62e0888678e3df
- Primary Source: MacStories (https://www.macstories.net/stories/a-closer-look-at-claudes-mac-apps/)
- Executive Summary: Anthropic has launched the 'Install as app' beta for Mac and Windows, allowing users to package Claude Artifacts into standalone desktop applications. Based on an Electron shim, these apps require the main Claude process to handle model interactions and system permissions, with files localized and indexed for OS-native integration.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Anthropic: Enables packaging Artifacts as standalone desktop applications using Electron, leveraging integrated Claude model and connector capabilities.
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To lower the barrier for deploying AI-generated code and bypass traditional distribution bottlenecks.
* [Key Fact Detail] Artifacts convertibility into standalone desktop apps with native icons/windows.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Strategic shift toward AI-native software distribution platforms.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the company’s blog:
> Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.
> When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.
> Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.
> If you’re an AppStories listener, you know that I’ve long thought it was only a matter of time until one of the big labs figured out how to turn their models’ frontier coding capabilities into a means to disrupt the App Store. This move feels like Anthropic’s first step in that direction.
> Before I get into the technical details, let me say this upfront: if I were Apple, I’d be very concerned that Anthropic is now shipping a nicely packaged system for users to make whatever app they want and turn Apple’s ecosystem into Claude’s ecosystem of tools and mods on their computers.
> Now, the way Anthropic made this happen can be debated, but I think the system is based on some clever engineering and savvy lock-in strategy. First, for these apps to work, you need the main Claude app to be installed and logged in with your account. These apps require the main Claude process to be running because every action they perform is actually handled by the Claude app behind the scenes, including permissions such as Full Disk Access. All apps made with Claude (either the ones you make, or the ones shared with you by other people) get installed at ~/Applications/Claude Apps, so they’re indexed by Spotlight and can be pinned to the macOS Dock. In fact, when you first create an app inside a Claude conversation (which can be a regular Claude session – you do not need to use Claude Code for these), there is a cute animation and install flow that puts an app directly in your Dock. It’s not too dissimilar from how the Shortcuts app can add individual shortcuts to your Mac’s Dock.
> Crucially, these are not native apps created with Swift or SwiftUI: they’re HTML apps, wrapped inside an Electron shim, which is entirely managed by Claude’s Chromium process for Electron. It’s somewhat reminiscent of Raycast’s Glaze product, which uses Vite/React web a...

### Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/426751942b8f186f
- Primary Source: Washington Post (https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/25/hegseth-pentagon-officials-floated-using-wartime-law-reappoint-nvidia-ceo/)
- Executive Summary: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Steve Feinberg explored invoking the 1950 Defense Production Act to pressure Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. The move was motivated by the administration’s perception of Nvidia as a national security pillar essential for maintaining dominance in the AI arms race against China.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Pete Hegseth (Defense Secretary), Steve Feinberg (Deputy), Jensen Huang (Nvidia CEO): Considering using the DPA as leverage to force a change in corporate governance
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Strategic necessity of AI dominance and national security concerns
* [Key Fact Detail] Administration officials explored the DPA to influence Nvidia's leadership.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Reflects aggressive policy intervention in the private tech sector.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea: invoking a Cold War-era law to pressure Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the debate.
> The Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that grants the president broad authority to intervene in the economy, has historically been used to mobilize private companies to supply the military in wartime or during national emergencies. The first Trump administration used the law to prompt General Motors to produce ventilators during the covid-19 pandemic.
> Before Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced Monday, Pentagon officials including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure Nvidia’s board to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive talks.
> News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free
> While the law provides no clear path to installing a new CEO, it could be used as a warning. “Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” said one of the three people, a Trump administration official. That could have curbed the chipmaker’s production plans and profit.
> The conversation about the law as part of a campaign to place Huang back in power, which has not been previously reported, reflects the intensity with which the military views the AI race with China and the lengths the Trump administration may be willing to go to intervene in the economy. It also reveals another dimension of the Defense Department’s growing entanglement with Silicon Valley: Though the DPA has never been used to install a leader in a private company, the idea has gained currency with some influential members of the tech sector in recent weeks.
> It is unclear what was ultimately conveyed to Nvidia, or whether those arguments made their way to President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, both of whom ultimately became convinced that Huang needed to be back in his job. The two were willing to use the powerful muscle of the federal government to make that happen, as part of a “full-court press” by Cabinet officials over the weekend, one of the people said. Hegseth and Feinberg were part of that campaign, according to two of the people.
> Government officials emphasized during the talks that restoring Huang was important for U.S. national security, but Nvidia’s board did not perceive it as a threat, according to a person familiar with the board’s thinking.
> The president and v...

Lending to data centers in the region surged in the following years, while chip financing was just beginning to take off more recently as banks got more comfortable with the riskier deals.
> That changed after the US announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need a US government license to purchase advanced AI chips from American manufacturers. Globally, data centers that already lease significant compute to Chinese firms will need a separate license to continue doing so and have a 90-day window to obtain it.
> More than a dozen bankers said their teams were waiting for answers on how the new curbs would affect borrowers and that would at the very least delay potential deals from going through. ### Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/dea16470e533c2f4
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1042221/google-my-channel-ai-video-patent)
- Executive Summary: Google's 'My Channel' patent details a system that utilizes user demographic, geolocation, and viewing history to generate personalized AI-driven video feeds. The technology includes concepts for creating digital avatars of users to feature them as protagonists in AI-generated narrative content.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Google: Filed a patent for real-time AI video generation based on user behavior and the creation of personalized digital avatars.
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To increase user engagement and advertising precision through highly customized AI-generated entertainment.
* [Key Fact Detail] Uses demographic, geolocation, and history data to generate personalized video content in real-time.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Aims to integrate streaming data to enhance AI-driven advertisement precision.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.
> First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.
> According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.
> Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.
> My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its use...

### Nvidia Agrees to Pay $290M to Settle Investor Lawsuit Over Crypto Mining Sales
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/dec9d4e18353ca87
- Primary Source: Reuters (https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/nvidia-agrees-settle-2018-us-investor-class-action-for-290-million-2026-11-25/)
- Executive Summary: Nvidia has agreed to a $290 million settlement to resolve a class-action lawsuit filed by investors, who alleged the company misled shareholders regarding the proportion of gaming GPU revenue driven by crypto mining during the 2017 boom. The case, which survived multiple legal challenges including Supreme Court dismissal of Nvidia's appeal, awaits preliminary court approval.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Nvidia, E. Ohman J:or Fonder AB (lead plaintiff) (US Federal District Court): $290 million settlement to resolve disclosure-related litigation
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Alleged failure to disclose crypto-mining-driven sales within gaming revenue during the 2017 crypto boom
* [Key Metrics] Nvidia has agreed to a $290 million settlement to resolve a class-action lawsuit filed by investors, who alleged the company misled shareholders regarding the proportion of gaming GPU revenue driven by crypto mining during the 2017 boom.
* [Official Stance & Demand] Industry outlook: Sets a strict disclosure precedent for hardware revenue reporting amidst volatile demand.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA) has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a long-running US investor lawsuit accusing the chipmaker of misleading shareholders about the role crypto mining played in its gaming business.
> The proposed settlement follows a lawsuit filed in 2018 by investors who claimed Nvidia failed to properly disclose how much of its graphics processing unit (GPU) revenue came from crypto miners rather than video game players, according to a court filing on Tuesday,
> The investors, led by Stockholm-based asset manager E. Ohman J:or Fonder AB, argued that Nvidia presented strong gaming revenue as evidence of demand from gamers while a significant portion of sales was driven by crypto mining.
> NYSE Parent ICE to Bring Hyperliquid-Based Perpetual Futures to US
> Bitwise Raises Bitcoin Price Forecast To $1.6 Million By 2036
> Survey Finds 90% Of Large Businesses Are Embracing Tokenized Money
> Moody's Assigns Investment-Grade Rating To Ripple's Stablecoin
> Stablecoin Firm RedotPay To Hold IPO By Year's End: Reports
> Nvidia denied wrongdoing as part of the agreement. The settlement still requires preliminary approval from a US judge before it can move forward.
> The case centers on Nvidia's sales during the 2017 crypto boom, when rising prices for Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO: $ETH) encouraged miners to buy large numbers of powerful GPUs.
> Although Nvidia introduced graphics cards specifically designed for crypto mining, investors alleged that miners also purchased GeForce gaming GPUs, helping drive reported gaming revenue higher.
> The issue became more apparent in 2018, when crypto prices fell and demand for mining hardware weakened. Nvidia subsequently lowered its revenue forecast, citing a sharp decline in crypto-related demand and excess inventory of gaming GPUs. The company's shares also came under pressure after the news.
> A federal district court initially dismissed the case in 2021, but an appeals court revived key claims in August 2023. The US Supreme Court later dismissed Nvidia's appeal in December 2024, allowing the case to return to the lower court.
> In March 2026, the court certified the lawsuit as a class action, covering investors who bought Nvidia shares between August 10, 2017, and November 15, 2018.
> Nvidia shares are currently trading at $142.97, down around 8% today.

### How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/de691b40864898f1
- Primary Source: Reuters (https://www.reuters.com/business/us-justice-department-did-not-open-probe-into-jensen-huang-before-reinstatement-2026-11-25/)
- Executive Summary: US Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang poses no national security risk without conducting a formal investigation, relying on findings from probe into clients like Super Micro and Megaspeed. This decision facilitated Huang's reinstatement by the Trump administration, despite bipartisan Congressional pushback demanding more rigorous scrutiny ahead of his scheduled testimony.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] AG Todd Blanche, CEO Jensen Huang: Cleared Huang of national security risks to expedite reinstatement
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Presidential mandate amidst ongoing client-side export investigations
* [Regulatory & Investigation Focus] DOJ clears CEO based on client export compliance review.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Upcoming testimony serves as critical scrutiny point for risk exposure.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar with the matter.
> Instead, Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the Justice Department’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
> That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was crucial to Blanche’s decision to tell Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security, said two of the people.
> Jensen Huang’s reinstatement has angered members of Congress — both Republicans and Democrats — who say it’s too soon to set aside questions about whether Nvidia or its CEO endangered US national security. The lack of any additional effort to examine their roles prior to Trump’s intervention will likely fuel a push for more investigations on Capitol Hill.
> Huang is due to testify next week.
> The Justice Department probes of Nvidia customers found no evidence that Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China, the two people said. Nvidia was not a target of those investigations and cooperated, providing documents, interviews and other data that helped lead to that conclusion, they added.
> There was also no counterintelligence probe of Huang himself. US spy agencies have gathered information on Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and alleged paramour of Jensen Huang suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, said two other people familiar with the effort. But the US had no details that would warrant a probe into the Nvidia CEO, they said.
> Counterintelligence investigations are run separately from criminal investigations and are aimed at monitoring and neutralizing national security threats, rather than building a case for indictment.
> Justice Department officials concluded that Nvidia and Huang had committed no wrongdoing and did not suspect its chief executive posed a national-security risk, two of the people familiar with the matter said.
> Trump and Vance conveyed that conclusion to Nvidia’s board, which decided to reinstate Huang, according to Trump’s account of events in a CNBC interview on Monday.

### US chip-access curbs and anti-distillation measures are reportedly already slowing Chinese AI labs
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/e8fc1d2db939924f
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/us-chip-access-curbs-and-anti-distillation-measures-are-reportedly-already-slowing-chinese-ai-labs/)
- Executive Summary: Restrictions on remote access to advanced chips and anti-distillation defenses from US-based model providers are widening the development gap between Chinese AI labs and US incumbents. Estimates from DeepSeek indicate a potential nine-month lag without distillation, forcing firms like Moonshot AI and Alibaba to pivot toward domestic silicon and intensified internal RL research.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, OpenAI, Anthropic: Restricting remote compute access and anti-distillation defenses, causing development delays
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Dual-layer bottlenecking of compute and technical knowledge to throttle China's AI progress
* [Key Metrics] Moonshot AI has already canceled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Firms pivoting to domestic silicon and RL as strategic countermeasures.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> The US is tightening its grip in the AI race with China, and the push is already having an effect, according to The Information. Chinese AI developers including Deepseek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba have been under pressure since September, squeezed by restrictions on Chinese firms' remote access to advanced Nvidia chips in foreign data centers and by successful anti-distillation measures from OpenAI and Anthropic.
> As a result, many ongoing projects are facing delays, the report says. Last month, Deepseek researchers internally estimated that their gap to top US models could grow from three to six months to nine months if distillation disappears completely. Moonshot AI has already canceled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia.
> Chinese firms are now looking for new workarounds, the publication reports. Some are trying to rent computing power through non-Chinese third parties, while companies such as MiniMax, Mihoyo, and Alibaba are leaning more heavily on domestic chips. They are also investing more in training data for their own reinforcement learning.

### WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/280e3ba7ecd8a54c
- Primary Source: TechCrunch (https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/25/whatsapp-now-lets-you-schedule-messages-in-group-and-individual-chats/)
- Executive Summary: Meta's WhatsApp has launched a global message scheduling feature, allowing users to schedule texts, images, and videos between 10 minutes and 14 days in advance via a long-press on the send button. The messages will execute even while the device is offline, closing the utility gap with Telegram and Signal.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Meta (WhatsApp): Released message scheduling for texts and media, including offline execution
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To standardize UX for business collaboration and cross-timezone messaging compared to rivals
* [Key Metrics] Scheduling support via long-press (10m to 14d window).
* [Key Position & Outlook] Bridging feature parity gaps to enhance professional utility.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats.
> The feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later.
> Users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message.
> Notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos.
> The feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams.
> WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out.

### Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/76e4579412b21f36
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-says-letting-ai-govern-society-would-be-a-bad-idea/)
- Executive Summary: Dario Amodei said it was "absurd"to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will"to AI systems. In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control. AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes,"Amodei wrote. Political decisions should stay
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Matthias Bastian: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Dario Amodei said it was "absurd"to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will"to AI systems.
* [Key Fact Detail] In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions.
* [Industry Analysis] Political decisions should stay.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Dario Amodei said it was "absurd"to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will"to AI systems.
> In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control.
> AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes,"Amodei wrote. Political decisions should stay in human hands, he argued, and he rejected handing power to AI as firmly as he rejected autocracy.
> [...] We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination on the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word to governance by AI, and I feel just as strongly that handing over governance to AI is a bad idea. Dario Amodei
> Automating specific tasks such as driving, developing cancer drugs, and writing software could benefit humanity, Amodei said, but that was a different matter from giving up free will in politics.
> ### Amodei says that full automation isn't always worth the risk
> End-to-end automation could also bring risks, Amodei wrote, including serious job disruption and AI building new models without human oversight. "It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,"he wrote. "But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it."In many cases, he added, "humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better."
> Amodei said AI companies didn't differ much on automating specific tasks. Some AI CEOs, he wrote, repeated slogans like "human control and agency"and "AI should be just a tool"but still shipped products built for more and more automation.
> Anthropic, by contrast, refused to allow its existing models to be used for autonomous weapons during its dispute with the Pentagon. He was "willing to risk Anthropic's future as a company"over that refusal, "even in the face of legal sanctions,"Amodei wrote.

### 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/e5f0d69d2c3df560
- Primary Source: TechCrunch (https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/25/1password-said-hackers-broke-into-its-internal-systems-but-customer-passwords-are-safe/)
- Executive Summary: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Zack Whittaker: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
* [Key Technical Spec] The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
* [Industry Analysis] The attacker used that employee.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
> The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
> The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.
> 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.
> In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.
> It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.
> 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.
> The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze’s privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.
> Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”
> The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.
> On December 1, a new privacy policy takes effect. It includes a table listing the types of “general personal information” that Backblaze says it has been collecting and sharing with third parties, including “advertising and marketing partners” since December 1, 2025, This information includes identifiers (such as “name, address, Internet Protocol address, [and] email address”); commercial information (such as “records of personal property, products or services purchased, obtained, or considered, or other purchasing or consuming histories or tendencies”; geolocation data that “can be used to determine a device’s physical location”; and “sensory or surveillance data” (which includes “call recordings or other audio, electronic, or visual monitoring or surveillance”).
> This has concerned some users, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:
> The Privacy Policy table lists one set of recipients across all data categories, which is why it can read differently. Our legal team will review the table for clarity as part of our next review cycle.
> ### No “sensitive personal information” shared
> Notably, no “sensitive personal information,” such as social security numbers, credit card numbers, or “precise geolocation,” is shared with advertisers, the policy states. However, identifiers, commercial information, “Internet or Other Similar Network Activity,” and “geolocation data” may be “sold or shared for targeted Advertising”
> Critically, the upcoming policy “only applies to the information collected in respect of your account and not to the content that you store on our system.” Backblaze’s broader terms of service also state that: “Files stored using Backblaze Computer Backup are encrypted prior to being sent to us.”

* [Core Event] Kai Nicol-Schwarz: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
* [Context & Motivation] Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
* [Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
> Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
> Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
> The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
> The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
> Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
> Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
> ### Scrutiny over Chinese access to Nvidia chips
> Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
> The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action,"sources previously told CNBC.
> In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
> U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box"on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
> "For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly,"he said.
> "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote ...
